title: Curated summary: How to read the oxalate table (University of Chicago Kidney Stone Program)
text:
How to read the oxalate table. Curated summary of the University of Chicago Kidney Stone Program article "How To Eat A Low Oxalate Diet", which links the program's "Updated table of oxalate foods". The oxalate numbers in this app's food table come from that table.
The table: the article says it is the Harvard list, reviewed by Dr Ross Holmes, with updated entries marked. Its numbers are mg of oxalate in a common portion: "The graph shows mg of oxalate in a common portion. The details of the portions are in the complete list." (Page section: "FOODS TO WORRY ABOUT".)
Portion size matters: "Note that quantity is critical." The article's example is black pepper: "black pepper is high in oxalate but the amounts used are small enough that total oxalate intake from it is negligible." (Opening section, about the lists.)
Daily goal: "If you do need a low oxalate diet, what is your goal? Less than 100 mg of diet oxalate is good; less than 50 mg is ideal." Also: "For stone prevention, a reasonable goal is below 100 mg of oxalate daily. An ideal would be about 50 mg daily if that can be accomplished." (Page section: "WHAT IS THE DIET OXALATE GOAL?".)
How to use the numbers: "To get there, consider the oxalate contents in common serving portions of all of the foods, and make up a plan for yourself." For the foods that most need attention: "The foods have in common that all contain at least 40 mg/serving." Many of the listed foods "can be used in your diet if you control the portion size and how often you use them." "Watch portions." "If you are eating one of the six dangerously high oxalate foods, stop eating it." The article says "Rhubarb and spinach are so high you just cannot eat them." (Page sections: "FOODS TO WORRY ABOUT", "FOODS TO AVOID", "WHAT ARE WE SAYING?".)
Category labels: the linked table also gives each food a category word. The article gives no mg cutoffs for those words, so use the mg number and its serving, not the word alone.
Calcium: have high-oxalate treats with milk "because calcium helps reduce oxalate absorption", and "There is every reason for stone formers to eat 1000 mg of calcium daily to protect their bones." (Page sections: "FOODS TO WORRY ABOUT" and "CALCIUM FIRST".)
Who needs it: "Do you need a low oxalate diet? You may if your stones contain calcium oxalate crystals and your urine oxalate is high enough to pose risk." (Page section: "DO YOU NEED A LIST?".)
Your own limit may be different. Follow the diet instructions from your doctor or dietitian.
curation_note: Team-written summary of the linked public page. Quoted sentences are verbatim and every number appears on that page; page sections are named in the text. Checked against snapshot uchicago-low-oxalate-diet.
